title: Pentecost
hookLine: the golden sequence: come, father of the poor

cards: The apostles are gathered in one place with Mary and some of the women, praying and waiting. Jerusalem outside is full of pilgrims for a harvest festival, the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover.
Then, Acts says, a sound from heaven like a mighty wind fills the whole house, and something appears like tongues of fire, resting on each one of them.

They spill out into the street speaking, and a crowd gathered from many nations hears them, each in their own language. Centuries later, someone wrote a song for this day, and the Church still sings it before the Gospel.

teach.b: Pentecost comes from the Greek for fiftieth: fifty days after Easter, the way the Jewish feast of weeks falls fifty days after Passover.

teach.h: TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.
teach.b: Acts describes it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire." On this day the Mass has a sequence, an old poem sung after the second reading.
The Missal's instructions require a sequence on just two days: Easter, and this one.

It's called the golden sequence, and it's usually credited to Stephen Langton, an archbishop of Canterbury, though nobody can prove he wrote it. It opens in Latin: "Veni, Sancte Spiritus." Come, Holy Spirit.
Then a run of lines, each one calling the Spirit by a new name. The first is "Veni, pater pauperum."
Come, father of the poor. Then giver of gifts, light of hearts, best comforter, the soul's sweet guest.

Later verses ask the Spirit to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is stiff, warm what is cold. Notice where it starts. Of all the names it could have used first, it chose the poor.

Not the powerful, not the learned. In Acts, the Spirit fell on a roomful of ordinary people, fishermen among them, and a few verses later the new community is selling what it owns and dividing it, as anyone had need.
The sequence remembers that, and puts the poor at the head of its list.

how: On Pentecost Sunday Catholics wear red at Mass, hear the story of the Spirit's coming in Acts 2, and sing or recite the sequence Veni, Sancte Spiritus before the Gospel; the Easter season ends that day.

o: the fortieth day, when Jesus went up
the fiftieth day, when the Spirit came
a Greek word for tongues of fire

s: the Church requires a sequence at every Sunday Mass
only two are required all year: at Easter and at Pentecost.
the sequence's first name for the Spirit is father of the poor
veni, pater pauperum comes right after the opening call.
we know for certain who wrote the golden sequence
it's usually credited to Stephen Langton, but nobody can prove it.

games.q: you're writing a song to call on the Holy Spirit. you've opened with come, Holy Spirit. which name comes next in the real sequence?
games.why: veni, pater pauperum: come, father of the poor. of all the names it could choose first, it chose the poor.

practice: Let your breathing slow and bring to mind one place in you that's dry, or cold, or stiff: a resentment, a tiredness, a door you've closed.
If you pray, you can say the old opening words on your breath, in Latin or English: Veni, Sancte Spiritus, come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, breathe in as if you were opening a window in that room.

wordCard.voice: Pentecost. Greek for fiftieth: the day fifty days after Easter when tongues of fire rested on the apostles and the golden sequence calls the Spirit by many names. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: come, Holy Spirit — the opening of the Pentecost sequence.

carryVoice: Your line: come, father of the poor. Wind, fire, and a roomful of ordinary people. Day six hundred seventy.
